summary: Defines optimizations to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for 6LoWPANs, such as IEEE 802.15.4 networks. These links make little use of multicast to save energy and may not follow normal IP subnet ideas. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6775 changes IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for low-power wireless networks. A host registers its address with a router instead of relying on routers to find it with multicast messages.

questions: ipv6 neighbor discovery for low-power wireless
what is the address registration option
how does 6lowpan duplicate address detection work
subtitle: Neighbor Discovery changes for low-power wireless nodes that sleep and cannot rely on multicast.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses multicast and assumes nodes are usually reachable, which wastes energy and can fail on low-power, lossy wireless links.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts register addresses with routers using unicast Neighbor Solicitations and a new Address Registration Option. Border routers can distribute prefixes and compression contexts and coordinate duplicate checks across hops.
tldr.outcome: The changes support sleeping hosts and update RFC 4944. RFC 6775 has been updated by RFC 8505, RFC 8929, and RFC 9010.

today: RFC 6775 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944. It has been updated by RFC 8505, RFC 8929, and RFC 9010.

sections.title: Why Low-Power Networks Need Different Discovery
sections.content:
6LoWPAN links can be lossy, low-power, and asymmetric, and many devices sleep for long periods. IPv6 Neighbor Discovery relies heavily on multicast and assumes nodes remain reachable, which is inefficient or impractical in these conditions.

RFC 6775 reduces multicast use, makes host-router exchanges host-initiated, adds address registration, distributes header-compression contexts, and defines mechanisms for multihop prefix distribution and duplicate-address detection. Its optimizations apply when nodes in the LoWPAN use them in a consistent way.
sections.plainLanguage: Small wireless devices may sleep and may not hear every neighbor. This RFC changes discovery so hosts ask routers for information and register their addresses directly.

sections.title: Hosts, Routers, and Network Layouts
sections.content:
A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) can be a host or router. A 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) forwards packets in a route-over network. A 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) sits at the network edge and is the authority for IPv6 prefix information.

In mesh-under topology, link-layer forwarding connects nodes to the 6LBR and there are no 6LRs. In route-over topology, intermediate IP routers carry packets toward the 6LBR. The host-to-router exchange is the same in both layouts.

Routing protocols may replace the RFC's multihop prefix/context distribution or multihop duplicate-address detection. If one of the prefix and context mechanisms is replaced, the other must also be replaced.
sections.plainLanguage: The 6LBR manages the network's prefixes, while 6LRs can forward traffic in route-over networks. Hosts use the same registration exchange regardless of which layout is used.

sections.title: Registration, Context, and Border-Router Messages
sections.content:
The Address Registration Option (ARO) carries a registration lifetime and the interface's EUI-64. A host includes it in a unicast Neighbor Solicitation; the router returns an Address Registration Option with a status in its Neighbor Advertisement.

The 6LoWPAN Context Option (6CO) carries a prefix, a context identifier, a validity period, and a flag controlling whether the context may be used for compression. The Authoritative Border Router Option (ABRO) identifies the 6LBR and versions the prefix and context information it originates.

For multihop duplicate-address detection, a 6LR sends a Duplicate Address Request (DAR) to a 6LBR and receives a Duplicate Address Confirmation (DAC). These are separate ICMPv6 messages because they cross routers and cannot use Neighbor Discovery's hop-limit check.
sections.plainLanguage: The ARO lets a host register an address and lets the router report the result. Other options carry compression context and identify which border router supplied network information.

sections.title: How a Host Finds a Router and Registers
sections.content:
A host sends a Router Solicitation to discover default routers and includes its source link-layer address so the router can answer by unicast. It must not multicast a Neighbor Solicitation.

After configuring an address, the host registers it with one or more default routers by sending a unicast Neighbor Solicitation with an ARO. It renews the registration before its lifetime expires and can deregister by sending a lifetime of zero.

A host can choose a registration lifetime that lasts through its sleep period. If a router reports a duplicate address, the host must not use that address. If a router's neighbor cache is full, the host should try another router.
sections.plainLanguage: A host asks a router to remember its address for a chosen time, then renews before that time ends. This lets the host sleep without requiring the router to search for it.

sections.title: How Routers and Border Routers Keep State
sections.content:
A router stores a registered address with its lifetime and EUI-64. If another device registers the same address with a different EUI-64, the router reports a duplicate without changing its neighbor entry. A registration with a zero lifetime removes the entry.

For multihop prefix and context distribution, a 6LBR increments the ABRO version when its information changes. A 6LR ignores information with an older version and keeps the ABRO associated with the prefixes and contexts it describes.

For multihop duplicate checking, a 6LR creates a tentative entry, sends a DAR to a 6LBR, and waits for a DAC. The 6LR changes its entry to registered only when a matching successful confirmation arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep a timed record of each registered address. Border routers identify their information with a version, and intermediate routers ignore older versions.

sections.title: Security Assumptions and Multihop Checks
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the link layer is sufficiently protected, for example with MAC-layer cryptography. Link-layer security protocols for 6LoWPAN are outside its scope.

DAR and DAC messages cross multiple hops, so the Neighbor Discovery hop-limit check does not apply. Routers must not change a neighbor cache because of a DAR, and may act on a DAC only when it matches a tentative entry. A router must discard these messages unless its interface is configured for the optimization.

The RFC notes that a rogue router can force DHCP use for non-EUI-64 addresses by setting the managed-address flag.
sections.plainLanguage: The design assumes the wireless link already has suitable protection. Because duplicate-check messages travel across routers, those messages cannot directly change neighbor records.
